# Joshua 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Overview

The chapter has four sections: (1) the allotment for Manasseh — the families and the daughters of Zelophehad (vv. 1–6); (2) the territorial boundaries of western Manasseh (vv. 7–11); (3) Manasseh's failure to drive out the Canaanites (vv. 12–13); and (4) the complaint of the "house of Joseph" and Joshua's reply (vv. 14–18).

---

## Verses 1–2: The Lot for Manasseh

**v. 1:** *"Now this was the allotment for the tribe of Manasseh as Joseph's firstborn son, namely for Machir the firstborn of Manasseh... because Machir was a man of war."*

- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the preferred translation is "and the lot for the tribe of Manasseh — for he was the firstborn of Joseph — fell to Machir." The point is that the proper possession of Manasseh fell to Machir's descendants because of their warlike spirit and numbers; they were sufficient to occupy Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan while the rest of the tribe received land west of Jordan. The phrase "for he was the firstborn of Joseph" is discussed as an explanation of why Ephraim and Manasseh are separate tribes, or why they are listed in this order since Ephraim was not the firstborn (cf. Genesis 48:5, 14). There is no "therefore" in the Hebrew for "therefore he had"; the literal is "and he had." — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

- Gill (Baptist) says Machir "very likely had shown his warlike disposition and courage in Egypt, and had fought under the kings there against the common enemy of that country; for it is highly probable he was dead before the children of Israel came out from thence, but the same warlike spirit continued in his posterity." The land was assigned to them on the east of Jordan to defend that territory while Reuben and Gad tended their flocks. — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

- Matthew Henry notes Manasseh was "divided and subdivided" — one part east of Jordan (Machir's posterity) and one part west. Machir "had signalized himself as a man of war, probably in the contests between the Ephraimites and the men of Gath (1 Chronicles 7:21)." — (Matthew Henry) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/joshua-17.html

- David Guzik (Enduring Word, broadly Pentecostal/charismatic evangelical) simply notes this was the westward allotment, the eastern portion having already been settled. — (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**v. 2:** *"…the rest of the descendants of Manasseh—the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida."*

- Gill notes these six families correspond to the Jeezerites, Helekites, Asrielites, Shechemites, Hepherites, and Shemidaites of Numbers 26:30. Abiezer is called Jeezer in Numbers 26:30; Gideon was of this family (Judges 6:11). — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

- Ellicott notes it is noteworthy that although the boundary in Joshua 16 suggests Shechem lay within Manasseh's border, as "the separate cities" of Ephraim were among Manasseh's inheritance (Joshua 16:9), this may have been the case with Shechem, the first metropolis of the Israelites in Palestine. — (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary clarifies: "The male children. Rather, the male descendants. None of the persons here mentioned were (Numbers 26:30, 31; 1 Chronicles 7:18) the sons of Manasseh." — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

---

## Verses 3–6: The Daughters of Zelophehad

**v. 3:** *"But Zelophehad son of Hepher… had no sons but only daughters. These are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah."*

- This case was first raised in Numbers 27 and further regulated in Numbers 36. Four times in Scripture the incident is recounted and the five daughters' names given in full, which is unusual. — (Expositor's Bible) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/joshua-17.html

- The Pulpit Commentary adds that the inheritance was given on condition that the daughters marry within their own tribe (Numbers 36), "a condition which was fulfilled. Thus the name of Zelophehad, and the portion of land belonging to him, was not blotted out from the memory of his descendants." — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

- Gill notes the genealogy is "particularly given, to show the truth and reality of it, upon which his daughters made their request." — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

**v. 4:** *"They approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders, and said, 'The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers.'"*

- David Guzik notes: "It was more important that the land remain in the ancestral families than it was to follow the custom that only males should inherit land." He cites Schaeffer: "They regarded the Pentateuch as the Word of God and as something that not only conveyed some sort of religious feeling, but also gave specific commands that were to be obeyed in detail." — (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

- Matthew Henry observes: "They had themselves, when they were young, pleaded their own cause before Moses, and obtained the grant of an inheritance with their brethren, and now they would not lose the benefit of that grant for want of speaking to Joshua, but seasonably put in their demand themselves… Joshua knew very well what God had ordered in their case, and did not object that they having not served in the wars of Canaan there was no reason why they should share in the possessions of Canaan." — (Matthew Henry) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/joshua-17.html

- The Pulpit Commentary: "They came near in order to demand the fulfilment of the decree of Moses just referred to, to which they appeal in support of their claim (see also Numbers 27:1-7)." — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

**v. 5:** *"Thus ten shares fell to Manasseh, in addition to the land of Gilead and Bashan beyond the Jordan."*

- The Pulpit Commentary: "Literally, and the measured portions of Manasseh fell ten (in number). It will be observed that the descendants of Manasseh, exclusive of Hepher, are five in number. These, with the five portions allotted to the family of Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, made up ten." — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

- Ellicott: "Ten portions — i.e., five for the sons named in Joshua 17:2, excepting Hepher, and five for Hepher's five grand-daughters." — (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm

- Gill mentions the rabbinic tradition (from the Talmud, Bava Bathra) that the six families had six parts, and the daughters had four parts — one for Zelophehad, two for Hepher (said to be the firstborn), and one for an uncle who died childless. But Gill rejects this: "the true case seems to be this, there were six portions for the six families, but there being no sons in Hepher's family, his part was divided into five, and given to the five daughters of Zelophehad." — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

**v. 6:** *"because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance among his sons. And the land of Gilead belonged to the rest of the sons of Manasseh."*

- The Pulpit Commentary explains that "the rest of Manasseh's sons" refers to the descendants of Machir (see v. 1), noting the ambiguity of "son" in Scripture (b'ne Israel = "sons of Israel" = "children of Israel"). — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

---

## Verses 7–11: The Borders of Western Manasseh

**v. 7:** *"Now the border of Manasseh went from Asher to Michmethath near Shechem, then southward to include the inhabitants of En-tappuah."*

- Ellicott: "Literally, from Asher-ham-Michmethah, a double name; Michmethah being taken as the plain of Mukhnah." The exact spot is unidentified, but the plain of Mukhnah runs nearly due south from Shechem. En-tappuah is identified as Yasûf. — (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary argues that "Asher" here is a city (identified as modern Yasir, about five hours from Nablous on the road to Beisan), not the tribe of Asher. However, the interpretation is debated. — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

- Gill simply calls it "a city of the tribe of Manasseh" and notes Jerome reported a village of this name fifteen miles from Neapolis (Shechem). — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

**v. 8:** *"The region of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but Tappuah itself, on the border of Manasseh, belonged to Ephraim."*

- Gill: "the whole territory that went by that name… all the fields and villages in it belonged to the tribe of Manasseh: but Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the children of Ephraim; and was one of those separate cities they had among the inheritance of the children of Manasseh." — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

- Matthew Henry: "There was great communication between this tribe and that of Ephraim. The city of Tappuah belonged to Ephraim, but the country adjoining to Manasseh." — (Matthew Henry) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/joshua-17.html

**v. 9:** *"From there the border continued southward to the Brook of Kanah. There were cities belonging to Ephraim among the cities of Manasseh…"*

- The Pulpit Commentary suggests some words may have fallen out of the Hebrew text. The LXX adds "Jariel" and translates differently. The point is that Ephraim had cities north of the brook within Manasseh's territory (see also Joshua 16:9). — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

- David Guzik calls this a pattern of intermingling between the two tribes. — (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**v. 10:** *"Ephraim's territory was to the south, and Manasseh's was to the north, having the Sea as its border and adjoining Asher on the north and Issachar on the east."*

- Ellicott: "Territorially, the tribe of Manasseh had the largest share of Palestine." He takes "Asher" here as referring to the tribe of Asher (whose territory extended south to Carmel), not Asher-ham-Michmethah, though he acknowledges Conder's view. The Manassites "touched Asher on the north, and Issachar on the east." — (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary engages in an extended discussion about the geography, arguing against Conder's view that would cut Manasseh's territory "almost in half." It contends that the contraction of Manasseh's territory "explains why cities had to be given to it out of Asher and Issachar, as well as the complaint in the latter part of this chapter." — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

**v. 11:** *"Within Issachar and Asher, Manasseh was assigned Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor (that is, Naphath), Endor, Taanach, and Megiddo, each with their surrounding settlements."*

- The Pulpit Commentary provides detailed notes on each city: Beth-shean (later Scythopolis, modern Beisan) had a citadel of "remarkable natural strength"; Endor (famous for Saul's witch) "is four miles south of Mount Tabor, in a country honeycombed with caves"; Megiddo and Taanach were royal Canaanite cities (Joshua 12:21). "Three countries" (BSB "Naphath") is better rendered "three hills" or elevated spots — Endor, Taanach, and Megiddo — which "make very nearly an equilateral triangle." — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

- Ellicott: "three countries" — the places named "do happen to lie on three distinct sheets of the map." — (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm

---

## Verses 12–13: Incomplete Conquest

**v. 12:** *"But the descendants of Manasseh were unable to occupy these cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in this land."*

- Ellicott: "Note the defalcation of Manasseh." — (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm

- Gill says they failed initially through "negligent and slothful" behaviour, and "afterwards it was too late, they became too strong and numerous for them." — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

- David Guzik: "It isn't a surprise that the Canaanites would be determined to remain in the land. What was lacking was complete determination from the people of Israel. They were satisfied to put the Canaanites to forced labor instead of driving them out." He quotes Howard: "They had the power to remove the Canaanites from the land and so to be God's instruments of judgment to remove wickedness, but they chose to tolerate wickedness and to use for their own purposes that which God had devoted to destruction. And so they sowed the seeds of their own destruction." — (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**v. 13:** *"However, when the Israelites grew stronger, they put the Canaanites to forced labor; but they failed to drive them out completely."*

- Gill states plainly: "they did not take away their lives, as they were commanded to do, but made them tributaries to them, which seems to arise from a covetous disposition, and done for the sake of gain: but did not utterly drive them out; which they were ordered to do, and could now have done; for if they were able to make them pay tribute to them, they had power sufficient to drive them out, or destroy them, and therefore broke the commandment of God, Deuteronomy 7:1." — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

- David Guzik says this failure followed "the same pattern as the failure of the tribe of Ephraim in Joshua 16:10." He adds: "this compromise, seemingly innocent, became the gateway to the idolatry and moral corruption that plagued Israel during the judges." — (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

---

## Verses 14–18: The Complaint of the House of Joseph

**v. 14:** *"Then the sons of Joseph said to Joshua, 'Why have you given us only one portion as an inheritance? We have many people, because the LORD has blessed us abundantly.'"*

- Ellicott calls this "the key to several difficulties in the Book of Joshua." He notes that "a large portion of the centre of Palestine consisted of uncleared forest" and this explains Israel's military strategy of striking the centre first to divide the Canaanite forces. He observes the arrogance of the Ephraimites, which "may be abundantly illustrated from Old Testament history, by the stories of their behaviour to Gideon and Jephthah, and even to David in later times." — (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm

- The Pulpit Commentary notes the tribe of Joseph outnumbered every tribe except Judah at the first census, and outnumbered them all by the plains of Moab census (Numbers 26). But "the demand… seems to have been a little unbecoming, since Joseph had obtained two lots and two portions, since half the tribe of Manasseh had settled on the east of Jordan." The Pulpit sees "covert sarcasm" in Joshua's reply. The complaint was likely driven by the idea "that Joshua, as one of themselves, ought to have taken more care of the interests of his own tribe." But Joshua "as a true servant of God" was above such favouritism. — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

- Matthew Henry: "It is probable, because Joshua was himself of the tribe of Ephraim, they promised themselves that they should have some particular favour shown them… but Joshua makes them know that in the discharge of his office, as a public person, he had no more regard to his own tribe than to any other, but would administer impartially, without favour or affection, wherein he has left an excellent example to all in public trusts." He notes the Greek word for "complainers" in Jude 1:16 is *mempsimoiroi*, "blamers of their lot." — (Matthew Henry) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/joshua-17.html

- David Guzik: "They challenged the outcome of the lot (goral), which was controlled by God. Thus, in their request they were challenging the very workings of God himself" (quoting Howard). — (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**v. 15:** *"Joshua answered them, 'If you have so many people that the hill country of Ephraim is too small for you, go to the forest and clear for yourself an area in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim.'"*

- Calvin (Reformed): "It is too apparent that they were thinking only of themselves, because they quibble as much as they can, in order to avoid following the suggestion of Joshua, than which, however, nothing was more reasonable." — (Calvin) https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom07/calcom07.xxviii.xvii.html

- Matthew Henry: "Many wish for larger possessions who do not cultivate and make the best of what they have, think they should have more talents given them who do not trade with those with which they are entrusted. Most people's poverty is the effect of their idleness; would they dig, they need not beg." — (Matthew Henry) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/joshua-17.html

- Gill: "if thou be a great people; which he does not deny, as they were for numbers and power: then get thee up to the wood country; which was near them, and within their borders… cut down the trees of the wood, clear the ground of them, and so make it habitable." — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

- David Guzik: Joshua's reply was "both wise and wonderful." He told them, "If you are a great people, then go and take the land for yourself; fully occupy what the LORD has given you." — (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

- Ellicott notes that "Perizzites" alongside "Rephaim (giants)" are mentioned together in Genesis 15:20 and a trace of the name Perizzite may survive in Ferasîn, west of Shechem. — (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm

**v. 16:** *"'The hill country is not enough for us,' they replied, 'and all the Canaanites who live in the valley have iron chariots, both in Beth-shean… and in the Valley of Jezreel.'"*

- Calvin: They "quibble as much as they can" — complaining the mountain is "rugged and little better than a desert" and that the fertile plain is barred by iron chariots, "as if they had not already learned by experience that the Lord was able, without any difficulty, to trample down both horses and chariots." — (Calvin) https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom07/calcom07.xxviii.xvii.html

- The Pulpit Commentary says this reply "justifies Joshua's sarcasm. The Ephraimites and Manassites blame Joshua when they ought to be blaming themselves. They excuse themselves from a task which they are too idle to execute." — (Pulpit Commentary) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/17.htm

- David Guzik: "The tribes of Joseph objected to Joshua's proposal. They complained that the wooded areas that could be cleared were not enough. They complained that the enemies on the plains were too strong with their chariots of iron… This was a different attitude compared to Caleb in Joshua 14:11–12. The men of Manasseh and Ephraim wanted a gift of 'easy land.'" — (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/

**v. 17:** *"So Joshua said to the house of Joseph—to Ephraim and Manasseh—'You have many people and great strength. You shall not have just one allotment.'"*

- Gill notes: "thou shalt not have one lot only; or only have what they were possessed of, but should have more; and, as they wanted more, they were able enough to get more." — (Gill) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html

- Matthew Henry: "He owns they were a great people, and being two tribes ought to have more than one lot only, but tells them that what had fallen to their share would be a sufficient lot for them both, if they would but work and fight." — (Matthew Henry) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/joshua-17.html

**v. 18:** *"because the hill country will be yours as well. It is a forest; clear it, and its farthest limits will be yours. Although the Canaanites have iron chariots and although they are strong, you can drive them out."*

- Spurgeon (Baptist), in a famous sermon on this text: "Our text is a war-speech to the tribes of Manasseh and Ephraim." He applies the "iron chariots" spiritually: "There are certain sins that, when we begin to war with them, we very soon overcome… but down in the plain, where there was plenty of room for horses and chariots, the Israelites were puzzled what to do; for some of these Canaanites had chariots of iron, which had scythes fixed to the axles, and when they drove into the ranks of an army, they mowed down the people as a reaping machine cuts down the standing corn… Dread made them powerless, till they plucked up courage." — (Spurgeon) https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/driving-out-the-canaanites-and-their-iron-chariots

- Ligonier (Reformed) explains the historical significance: "Iron significantly outclassed all of the other materials used for military purposes. Moreover, chariots contributed dynamically to engagements in the lowlands. Israel did not possess chariots, and when they encountered these fortified war machines on the plains, it resembled an engagement between foot soldiers and tanks." Yet Joshua guaranteed victory because of God's pledge going back to Exodus 23. — (Ligonier) https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/chariots-of-iron

- Calvin: "Joshua, however, by a simple and right-hearted answer, administers due castigation, as well to their avarice as their effeminacy and torpor. If the forest, as it now stands, is not sufficiently productive, cut down the trees and convert it into good fields; provided you are not sparing of your labor, you will have no reason to be dissatisfied with your habitation. Iron chariots, moreover, cannot prevent the Lord from performing what he has promised to you." — (Calvin) https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom07/calcom07.xxviii.xvii.html

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The differences among Protestant traditions on this chapter are largely in **application and emphasis** rather than in exegetical conclusions about the text itself. All major commentators agree on the historical meaning.

**Reformed (Calvin / Ligonier):** Emphasises God's sovereignty in the lot ("controlled by God") and human responsibility. Calvin stresses that the Ephraimites' complaint was sinful because it challenged God's providence and revealed "avarice," "effeminacy," and "torpor." The iron chariots were no obstacle if God was trusted. Ligonier connects this to spiritual warfare today: "Our Savior has crushed the head of our enemy." (https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/chariots-of-iron; https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom07/calcom07.xxviii.xvii.html)

**Baptist (Spurgeon / Gill):** Spurgeon makes a strongly applicatory, evangelistic use of v. 18 — iron chariots represent besetting sins that believers fear to face. His sermon focuses on the psychology of fear: "Dread made them powerless, till they plucked up courage." Gill emphasises the covenantal and historical precision — the breach of Deuteronomy 7:1 was deliberate sin. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/driving-out-the-canaanites-and-their-iron-chariots; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-17.html)

**Non-conformist / Presbyterian (Matthew Henry):** Stresses the practical and moral lesson — "Most people's poverty is the effect of their idleness; would they dig, they need not beg." Henry sees Joshua as a model of impartial public leadership: "he had no more regard to his own tribe than to any other." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/joshua-17.html)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Emphasises the importance of fully possessing what God has given: "Before asking for more, occupy completely what God has already granted." On the daughters of Zelophehad, Guzik highlights the trustworthiness of Scripture as a "specific command to be obeyed in detail." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-15-16-17/)

**Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch):** The Keil & Delitzsch commentary (standard conservative Lutheran reference) identifies the ten portions as five male and five female families, noting the text is from a unified tradition. (The full text was unavailable to fetch, but the excerpt confirms the reading.)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott approaches with historical-geographical precision and a literary eye. He notes the Ephraimites' arrogance as a recurring national trait traceable through Judges into the monarchy. He observes that vv. 14–18 provide "the key to several difficulties in the Book of Joshua" regarding Israel's military strategy. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/joshua/17.htm)

---

## Other Views

### Modern / Source-Critical Scholarship

- **Peake's Commentary** states that Joshua 17:1–10 is from a Priestly writer. It notes: "The only point of interest is the assignment of inheritance to the daughters of Zelophehad in accordance with Numbers 27:1 ff. There Moses ordains that the daughters of a man who has no sons shall take their father's inheritance. This is in opposition to ancient law, which recognised the sons only as heirs. Later feeling was against this, and the writer of Numbers 27:1 ff. gave effect to it by the imaginary instance of Zelophehad and his daughters. For a discussion of this kind of 'legal fiction,' see W. R. Smith, OTJC², p. 386." Peake further argues that vv. 14–18 show "the oldest tradition knew nothing of any territory E. of the Jordan being assigned to Manasseh by Moses," since the Joseph tribes claim they have "but one lot." The settlements east of Jordan would therefore be later than the western ones. — (Peake's Commentary) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/joshua-17.html

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

No dedicated Catholic or Orthodox verse-by-verse commentary on Joshua 17 was found within the specified search limits. The search for newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org returned no results specific to this chapter.

### "Legal Fiction" and the Daughters of Zelophehad

The Expositor's Bible (though not from the sites specified for "modern scholarship," contains relevant discussion) treats the case as a significant advance in women's property rights: "The incident is interesting, because it shows a larger regard to the rights of women than was usually conceded at the time. Some have, indeed, found fault with the decision as not going far enough… The answer to this objection is, that had the rights of women been recognised to this extent, it would have been too great an advance on the public opinion of the time. It was not God's method to enjoin laws absolutely perfect, but to enjoin what the conscience and public opinion of the time might be fairly expected to recognise and support." — (Expositor's Bible) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/joshua-17.html

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across the Chapter

1. **God's faithfulness to His Word:** The daughters of Zelophehad received their inheritance because God had commanded it through Moses — the Pentateuch was treated as binding, detailed instruction.
2. **The danger of partial obedience:** Manasseh's failure to drive out the Canaanites (vv. 12–13) mirrored Ephraim's (Joshua 16:10) and sowed seeds of future idolatry and judgment.
3. **Human excuses versus faith:** The Joseph tribes complained about insufficient land and iron chariots; Joshua replied that their problem was not lack of resources but lack of faith and effort.
4. **The principle of fully possessing what God has given:** Before asking for more, believers must occupy what they already have — a principle applied across all Protestant traditions.
